source_text: Qui status fidei, quae ratio ueritatis, quod praescriptum disciplinae inter cetera saecularium errorum etiam spectaculorum uoluptates adimat, dei serui, cognoscite, qui cum maxime ad deum acceditis, recognoscite, qui iam accessisse uos testificati et confessi estis, tne aut ignorando, aut dissimulando quis peccet. tanta est enim uoluptatium uis, ut et ignorantiam protelet in occasionem et conscientiam corrumpat in dissimulationem. ad utrumque adhuc forsan alicui opiniones ethnicorum blandiantur, qui in ista causa aduersus nos ita argumentari consuerunt: nihil obstrepere religioni in animo et in conscientia tanta solacia extrinsecus oculorum uel aurium nec uero deum offendi oblectatione hominis, qua saluo erga deum metu et honore suo in tempore et suo in loco frui scelus non sit. atquin hoc cum maxime paramus demonstrare, quemadmodum ista non competant uerae religioni et uero obsequio erga uerum deum. sunt qui existimant Christianos, expeditum morti genus, ad hanc obstinationem abdicatione uoluptatium erudiri, quo facilius uitam contemnant amputatis quasi retinaculis eius nec desiderent, quam iam superuacuam sibi fecerunt, ut hoc consilio potius et humano prospectu, non diuino praescripto definitum existimetur. pigebat scilicet etiam perseuerantes tantis in uoluptatibus propter dominum mori. quamquam etsi, ita esset tam apto consilio tantum obstinatio disciplinae debebat obsequium.
thought_title: The danger of pleasure and the pagan defense of shows
orientation: Tertullian opens his treatise by addressing fellow Christians and stating that the pleasures of the shows must be taken away from them, before quoting the pagan objection that such pleasures do not offend God.
pass_a_gloss: What the state of faith is, what the reason of truth is, what the prescription of discipline among the other errors of the world also takes away the pleasures of the shows, servants of God, know; you who are now especially drawing near to God, recognize; you who have testified and confessed that you have already drawn near, lest anyone sin either by not knowing or by pretending not to know. For so great is the force of pleasures that it both prolongs ignorance into an occasion and corrupts conscience into pretense. For both of these perhaps still the opinions of the pagans flatter someone, who in this case against us have been accustomed to argue thus: that nothing obstructs religion in the mind and in the conscience, such great solaces of the eyes or ears from outside; and that God is not offended by the amusement of a person, by which, with fear toward God and his own honor safe, to enjoy it in its own time and in its own place would not be a crime. But this is exactly what we are preparing to demonstrate, how these things do not belong to true religion and to true obedience toward the true God. There are those who think that Christians, a race ready for death, are trained to this obstinacy by the renunciation of pleasures, so that they may more easily despise life, having cut away as it were its reins, and may not desire what they have already made superfluous for themselves, so that this may be thought to have been determined by this plan rather and by human foresight, not by divine prescription. It would be irksome, of course, even for those persevering in such great pleasures to die for the Lord. Although even if it were so, such great obstinacy of discipline ought obedience to so fitting a plan.

choices.why: Keeps the glossary term 'shows' for spectacula and renders uoluptates as 'pleasures' per the glossary for uoluptas.
Direct address to the audience; 'servants of God' is the natural literal rendering.
Uses the glossary English for ethnici.
Literal rendering of the genitive phrase; 'amusement' captures the sense of oblectatio as a passing pleasure.
Literal rendering of the phrase; 'ready for death' captures expeditum morti as prepared or unencumbered for death.
Uses the glossary sense of renuntiatio-related abdicatio and 'pleasures' for uoluptates.

pass_b_english: Servants of God, understand the state of faith, the principle of truth, and the rule of discipline that, among the other errors of the world, also takes away the pleasures of the shows. You who are now drawing near to God, recognize it. You who have already testified and confessed that you have drawn near, recognize it, so that no one sins through ignorance or through pretending not to know. For the force of pleasures is so great that it both prolongs ignorance into an occasion for sin and corrupts conscience into pretense.

Against both of these, perhaps the opinions of pagans still flatter some people. In this matter they are accustomed to argue against us in this way: they say that such great comforts for the eyes and ears from outside do not obstruct religion in the mind and conscience, and God is not offended by the amusement of a person, since enjoying it at its proper time and in its proper place, with fear and honor toward God preserved, is not a crime.

But this is exactly what we are preparing to demonstrate: how these things do not belong to true religion and true obedience toward the true God. There are some who think that Christians, a race ready for death, are trained to this obstinacy by the renunciation of pleasures, so that they may more easily despise life once its reins, so to speak, have been cut away, and may not desire what they have already made superfluous for themselves. In this way it is supposed to be determined by human planning and foresight rather than by divine command. Of course it was irksome even for those who persevere in such great pleasures to die for the Lord. And yet, even if it were so, only with so fitting a plan did the obstinacy of discipline owe obedience.

problems.quote: prolongs ignorance into an occasion for sin
problems.why: 'protelet' means 'covers/protects/shields', not 'prolongs'; ignorance is shielded, not prolonged.
problems.fix: shields ignorance as an occasion for sin

problems.quote: As if it were irksome even for those who persevere in such great pleasures to die for the Lord.
problems.source_quote: pigebat scilicet etiam perseuerantes tantis in uoluptatibus propter dominum mori.
problems.why: 'pigebat' is imperfect 'it was irksome/displeasing', but the sense is ironic: 'Of course it would be irksome...' The English 'As if' captures irony but shifts from imperfect to conditional.
problems.fix: Of course it was irksome even for those who persevere in such great pleasures to die for the Lord.
problems.ruling: Latin states it was irksome; English adds 'As if', altering meaning

problems.quote: such a fitting plan would still owe its obstinacy of discipline to obedience.
problems.source_quote: tam apto consilio tantum obstinatio disciplinae debebat obsequium
problems.why: 'tam apto consilio' is ablative 'with so fitting a plan'; 'tantum' = 'only/so much' is adverbial, not 'its'. The sentence means: only with so fitting a plan did the obstinacy of discipline owe obedience.
problems.fix: even if it were so, only with so fitting a plan did the obstinacy of discipline owe obedience.
problems.ruling: Latin includes 'only' (tantum) and past sense (debebat); English omits and changes mood

edits.old: prolongs ignorance into an occasion for sin
edits.new: shields ignorance as an occasion for sin

edits.old: As if it were irksome even for those who persevere in such great pleasures to die for the Lord.
edits.new: Of course it was irksome even for those who persevere in such great pleasures to die for the Lord.

edits.old: such a fitting plan would still owe its obstinacy of discipline to obedience.

fixed: Changed 'prolongs ignorance into an occasion for sin' to 'shields ignorance as an occasion for sin' because 'protelet' means 'covers/protects/shields', not 'prolongs'.
Changed 'As if it were irksome...' to 'Of course it was irksome...' because 'pigebat' is imperfect indicative, and the source uses 'scilicet' ironically, not a conditional.

Changed 'such a fitting plan would still owe its obstinacy of discipline to obedience' to 'only with so fitting a plan did the obstinacy of discipline owe obedience' because 'tam apto consilio' is ablative 'with so fitting a plan' and 'tantum' is adverbial 'only/so much', not 'its'.

problems.quote: such great comforts for the eyes and ears from outside do not obstruct religion
problems.why: Pagan objection introduced without clear quotation marks or attribution.

problems.quote: the force of pleasures is so great that it both shields ignorance as an occasion for sin
problems.why: 'Shields ignorance' is odd; usually pleasure exposes or excuses ignorance.

edits.old: such great comforts for the eyes and ears from outside do not obstruct religion
edits.new: They say that such great comforts for the eyes and ears from outside do not obstruct religion

edits.old: it both shields ignorance as an occasion for sin
edits.new: it both prolongs ignorance into an occasion for sin

fixed: Added 'They say that' to mark the pagan objection as reported speech, since the source introduces it with 'argumentari consuerunt' (they are accustomed to argue).

Restored 'prolongs ignorance into an occasion for sin' to match the source 'ignorantiam protelet in occasionem' (prolongs ignorance into an occasion); 'shields' was a previous edit that misread 'protelet'.

last_rejected.quote: recognize it; you who have already testified and confessed that you have drawn near, recognize it
last_rejected.source_quote: recognoscite, qui iam accessisse uos testificati et confessi estis
last_rejected.why: The second 'recognoscite' is missing; source repeats the command to those already confessed.
last_rejected.fix: recognize it; you who have already testified and confessed that you have drawn near, recognize it again
last_rejected.ruling: English includes 'recognize it' for both groups, matching Latin imperatives cognoscite and recognoscite

polish.changed: Clarified the opening sentence by separating the three items of faith, truth, and discipline; marked the pagan objection as a distinct voice and closed it clearly before Tertullian resumes; smoothed sentence order and rhythm for reading aloud while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.quote: that such great comforts for the eyes and ears from outside do not obstruct religion
notes.why: Pagan objection introduced with 'who in this matter are accustomed to argue against us in this way' but not clearly closed; reader may lose track of whose voice resumes.
notes.fix: Close quotation more explicitly before 'But this is exactly what we are preparing to demonstrate'.

notes.quote: Servants of God, know what condition of faith, what principle of truth, what rule of discipline among the other errors of the world also takes away the pleasures of the shows
notes.why: Syntax convoluted; 'among the other errors of the world also takes away' is unclear—does faith take away pleasures, or is this a list?
notes.fix: Recast: 'know that the condition of faith...also takes away, among the other errors of the world, the pleasures of the shows'.

polish.changed: Clarified the pagan objection by introducing it as direct speech, smoothed the sentence about pleasure's force to show it prolongs ignorance and corrupts conscience, and made the final rhetorical point about discipline's obedience read naturally.
